title: Global liquidity peaks: the companies that spent most aggressively on AI in H1 are discounted first
dek: A rising capital market needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that invested most aggressively in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
why: It puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPOs and household balance sheets on the same funding chain, a macro framework that does not treat AI as a panacea.
who: For investors watching both US AI stocks and China/Hong Kong asset allocation, and for private-market practitioners judging the sources and pace of hot money in 2025.
skip: The discussion of individual Hong Kong IPO cases can be skipped; the main thread starts at 8:11 with Nvidia's liquidity experiment.

points.h: A low IPO break rate is not a good signal
points.body: Do not take the low first-day break rate of Hong Kong IPOs as a sign of a stronger market. In the first half of this year the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly fifty-fifty level normal under a market mechanism, meaning the main participants in IPOs were short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently the supply of listed companies has decreased, and IPO-related funds have blown up, yet the two newly listed companies still broke issue, showing that temporary supply-side control has not solved the fundamental problem: Hong Kong also faces peak liquidity.

points.h: The more aggressively you bet on AI, the sooner you are punished
points.body: Market attitude reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI CapEx, the higher the valuation; by the time half-year reports were concentratedly disclosed at the end of July, any large internet company that had made aggressive capital expenditures in the first half, especially those that spent all their free cash flow, was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was exactly the quarter of the most FOMO across the entire supply chain, with everyone afraid of price increases and rushing to spend money first, while inventory could still support gross margins; by Q3 inventory is exhausted and the impact of price increases returns, and unfavorable factors will appear together.

points.h: Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
points.body: Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco introduced "lease-to-buy" to help customers finance, recognizing future revenue as sales revenue in advance; Nvidia now also promotes lease-to-buy. In the financial report, free cash flow halved quarter-on-quarter, and accounts receivable on the books are far above historical levels—this is suspected to be partly related to the credit enhancement and collection structure brought by lease-to-buy. Therefore Nvidia may have reached a stage where it needs more aggressive financial tactics to maintain capital market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

points.h: Private-market money comes from bullets fired three years ago
points.body: The answer lies in the fundraising timing of funds. The money concentrated in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022; they barely invested in 2023-2025, until they saw state capital betting during a period when no one dared to invest and earning the most—the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large models, and two large chips stimulated market-based funds, and everyone's mentality was: copy the state capital's homework. So this is not a rational long-term increment, but more like a delayed emotional release.

points.h: New property policy removes households from the financing chain
points.body: The key to recent real estate policy is not to save developers, but to pull households out of the old financing cycle. In the past, buying pre-sale housing meant households played the role of financing targets in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive housing later; after the policy pushes the chain toward marketization, buyers get completed housing and only bear the consumer role, with risk reset back to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when housing prices were near the bottom, in order to first stabilize the denominator on the asset side and avoid panic from dismantling the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and the consolidation of China's coal and mining industries have followed similar paths.

points.h: A slow bull is not a slogan, it is a chip structure
points.body: A slow bull does not rely on slogans, but on layering market chips by duration: the bottom layer is low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips taken up by insurance, as long money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, performing a quasi-stabilizing function; Central Huijin and China Securities Finance adjust the index at a higher layer; the top layer is retail investors, private funds and active management money. The new insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in term, yield and liquidity, which institutionally ensures long money for long investment, medium money for medium investment, short money for short investment—not allowing ordinary people's short money to be invested in ten-year low-liquidity assets.

points.h: Crises are rescued ever bigger, at least one and a half bubbles
points.body: After the US dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks became increasingly accustomed to using money printing to directly intervene in crises, acting faster each time. The quantitative easing after 2008 should have been cleared during the rate hike cycle, but was interrupted by political intervention, and then the pandemic hit in 2020, so a larger flood of money was layered on top before the previous bubble had dissipated—today at least one and a half bubbles have accumulated. Central bank governors have learned to print more money immediately when a crisis first appears, and the endogenous result is that inflation, rising financial assets and wealth polarization intensify simultaneously. As long as the bubble is not allowed to clear, the world may face long-term stagflation in some form.

quotes.text: The reason I say it feels a bit precarious is that today the whole world has a bit of a problem with liquidity peaking.
In the capital market, whoever spends aggressively is seen as impressive, and then when everyone publishes half-year reports, it becomes whoever is aggressive gets punished.
Perhaps Nvidia has also reached a point where it needs to use lease-to-buy to drive revenue growth and meet capital market expectations.
Everyone looks and says, you can pull off this story like that, then I can definitely pull off this story like that too—psychologically it's roughly like that.
The so-called slow bull we always talk about is not because it is inherently both slow and bullish; it needs to first build a chip structure on the basis of a slow bull.
When the bubble piled up last time had not yet dissipated, a bigger one was added on top—and added without hesitation.
